text: You already know az vm create and aws ec2 run-instances from the earlier Azure and AWS courses. What's different in this lesson is intent: deploying a real VM or EC2 instance into the VNet/subnet and NSG, or VPC/subnet and security group, that Chapter 2 already built and Lesson 8 already verified — not into whatever network the platform defaults to.

az vm create takes --vnet-name and --subnet to put the instance's NIC inside snet-app-tier, the subnet Chapter 2 built for this tier, instead of a new default VNet Azure would otherwise create. --nsg attaches the NSG Lesson 7 configured. --public-ip-address with an empty string tells Azure not to create the public IP it would otherwise provision automatically — this subnet is private, and the VM has no business being reachable from the internet directly.

run-instances works the same way. --subnet-id places the instance's network interface inside the exact private subnet Chapter 2 built, and --security-group-ids attaches the security group Lesson 7 defined for this tier, instead of the account's default VPC and default security group. Because that subnet's route table has no route to an internet gateway, the instance gets no public IP no matter what auto-assign setting is on, the same public-private distinction from the AWS compute chapter.

Omit those flags and the launch doesn't fail — the platform quietly substitutes a default: AWS's default VPC and subnet, or a brand-new VNet Azure creates on the fly. The instance boots successfully, which is the real problem. It's running, it looks fine, and it's sitting on a network nobody designed, with none of Chapter 2's NSG or security group rules applied. That gap almost always surfaces later, as an unreachable instance or an unexpectedly open one — a worse time to find it than at launch.

Naming the exact subnet and NSG, or subnet and security group, at creation time is what turns a generic VM or EC2 launch into a deployment into this specific environment. Next up: deploying the storage account or S3 bucket this compute will actually use, configured private by default with access granted only where it's genuinely needed.
